subject: sociology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Modernisation theory broadly argues that poor countries remain underdeveloped because of what?
options: The activities of TNCs
The legacy of colonialism
Exploitation by rich nations
Internal cultural and economic barriers to 'modern' values
questions.explain: Modernisation theory locates the causes of underdevelopment internally, in traditional values and lack of modern institutions, and prescribes Western-style development.

questions.q: The 'embourgeoisement' thesis claimed that:
options: The middle class was being proletarianised by deskilling
Affluent manual workers were becoming middle class in values and lifestyle
Class had ceased to exist altogether
The bourgeoisie was shrinking under monopoly capitalism
questions.explain: The embourgeoisement thesis suggested affluent workers were adopting middle-class norms, a claim challenged by Goldthorpe and Lockwood's Affluent Worker study.

questions.q: What is a Transnational Corporation (TNC)?
options: A company operating and producing across many countries
A government department
A small local business
A national charity
questions.explain: TNCs are large firms that operate, produce and trade across national borders, and are central to debates about globalisation and development.

questions.q: The social democratic view of the welfare state holds that welfare should:
options: Promote greater equality and meet need through universal, state-provided services
Be minimal to avoid dependency
Be provided only through private markets
Be abolished in favour of charity
questions.explain: Social democrats see collective, often universal, welfare provision as a means of reducing inequality and guaranteeing rights of citizenship.

questions.q: In stratification debates, the 'feminisation of poverty' refers to:
options: The increasing proportion of those in poverty who are women
The decline of female employment
Women escaping poverty faster than men
Welfare benefits favouring women
questions.explain: The feminisation of poverty describes women's disproportionate vulnerability to poverty, linked to caring roles, low pay and lone parenthood.

questions.q: Andre Gunder Frank described the relationship at the heart of dependency theory as one between which two parts?
options: The metropolis (core) and the satellite (periphery)
The emic and the etic
Church and sect
The sacred and the profane
questions.explain: Frank argued surplus flows from satellite (peripheral) regions to the metropolis (core), keeping the periphery dependent and underdeveloped.

questions.q: What does 'glocalisation' describe?
options: The adaptation of global products and ideas to fit local cultures
A retreat from globalisation
The banning of foreign goods
The total replacement of local cultures
questions.explain: Glocalisation describes how global products, brands and ideas are modified and reinterpreted to suit local tastes and contexts.

questions.q: The 'culture of poverty' thesis, associated with Oscar Lewis, explains the persistence of poverty by arguing that:
options: The poor develop fatalistic values and norms that are passed on and trap them in poverty
Welfare benefits are too low
Poverty results from labour market discrimination
The poor are exploited by capitalism
questions.explain: Lewis argued the poor adapt by developing a self-perpetuating subculture of fatalism and present-time orientation that reproduces poverty.

questions.q: Which of the following best describes 'intergenerational mobility'?
options: Movement between countries
Movement only within the middle class
Movement during a single person's own career
Movement in class position between parents and their children
questions.explain: Intergenerational mobility compares an individual's class position with that of their parents.

questions.q: Which concept did Weber use to describe groups restricting access to rewards and opportunities to maintain their advantage?
options: Embourgeoisement
Pauperisation
Social closure
Polarisation
questions.explain: Social closure refers to the process by which status groups monopolise resources and exclude outsiders.

questions.q: Critics of TNCs argue that, in developing countries, they often do what?
options: Always raise wages to Western levels
Refuse to invest at all
Eliminate all global inequality
Exploit cheap labour and extract profits to richer nations
questions.explain: Dependency-influenced critics argue TNCs use cheap labour and resources while repatriating profits, reinforcing global inequality.

questions.q: Charles Murray's concept of the 'underclass' explains the position of the poorest mainly in terms of:
options: Discrimination by the welfare state against minorities
Exploitation by global capitalism
Structural unemployment caused by deindustrialisation
A dependency culture and inadequate socialisation, especially the rise of lone parenthood
questions.explain: Murray, a New Right thinker, argued an underclass develops a culture of welfare dependency, with illegitimacy and worklessness transmitted through poor socialisation.

questions.q: Manuel Castells argues that contemporary society is best understood as what?
options: A network society organised around information flows
A traditional agrarian society
A society without media
A purely industrial society
questions.explain: Castells argues digital information networks now structure economic, political and social life, producing the 'network society'.

questions.q: What is Tumin's main criticism of the Davis and Moore functionalist theory of stratification?
options: It reduces all inequality to patriarchy
It ignores that some unrewarded roles are also functionally important and that inequality blocks talent
It overstates the role of coercion in maintaining order
It assumes class is based purely on market position
questions.explain: Tumin argued that functional importance is hard to measure and that stratification actually prevents the discovery of talent by restricting opportunity.

questions.q: The Marxist concept of 'proletarianisation' suggests that:
options: Sections of the middle class (e.g. routine white-collar workers) are being deskilled into the working class
The bourgeoisie is expanding
Manual workers are becoming middle class
Class is disappearing
questions.explain: Proletarianisation argues that deskilled clerical and routine non-manual work has lost its middle-class character and resembles working-class labour.

questions.q: Defenders of modernisation theory argue development is helped by which of the following?
options: Adopting Western technology, education and entrepreneurial values
Cutting all ties with richer nations
Abolishing markets
Restricting all trade
questions.explain: Modernisation theory advocates adopting modern (often Western) values, education, technology and capitalist enterprise to promote development.

questions.q: Cultural 'hybridity' in globalisation theory refers to what?
options: Strict cultural separation
The blending of different cultures to create new mixed forms
The decline of all culture
A single dominant world culture
questions.explain: Hybridity describes the creation of new cultural forms from the mixing of previously separate cultures, as in fusion music or food.

questions.q: Which of the following is a key feature of official social class schemes such as the NS-SEC?
options: They are based on self-assigned class identity
They measure status honour directly
They classify people by their assets only
They classify the population by occupation and employment relations
questions.explain: Official class schemes such as the NS-SEC classify people primarily according to their occupation and employment relations.

questions.q: The pluralist view of the distribution of power argues that:
options: Power is held by a self-recruiting elite
Power is concentrated in a single ruling elite
Power belongs solely to the owners of capital
Power is dispersed among competing groups, none of which dominates
questions.explain: Pluralists argue power is spread across many competing interest groups, with the state acting as a neutral referee.

questions.q: Much of the upward absolute mobility seen in the mid-20th century is best explained by:
options: The abolition of the class system
Falling birth rates among the middle class
Expansion of professional and white-collar jobs (changes in the occupational structure)
A genuine increase in equality of opportunity
questions.explain: Structural changes that expanded non-manual jobs created 'more room at the top', producing upward mobility without necessarily greater fairness.

questions.q: Which writer is most associated with the New Right concept of the 'underclass'?
options: Peter Townsend
Charles Murray
Stanley Cohen
Erik Olin Wright
questions.explain: Charles Murray popularised the underclass thesis, attributing poverty to a dependency culture rather than structural factors.

questions.q: Weber argued that stratification should be understood through three distinct dimensions. These are:
options: Class, status and party
Power, authority and coercion
Wealth, income and welfare
Class, gender and ethnicity
questions.explain: Weber identified class (economic/market situation), status (social honour) and party (organised power) as separate but interlinked dimensions of stratification.

questions.q: Wallerstein's world-systems theory divides the global economy into which three zones?
options: Sacred, profane and secular
Core, semi-periphery and periphery
North, central and south
First, second and third worlds only
questions.explain: Wallerstein argued the capitalist world-system is structured into core, semi-periphery and periphery, with the semi-periphery as a buffer.

questions.q: Which of the following is the strongest example of 'global risk' in Beck's sense?
options: A local council election
A single household budget
Climate change affecting all nations
A local sports result
questions.explain: Climate change is a classic 'manufactured' global risk: it is human-caused, crosses borders and affects rich and poor societies alike.

questions.q: How does the Weberian concept of 'status' differ from 'class'?
options: Status applies only to the working class
Status and class are identical in Weber's scheme
Status is purely economic while class is about lifestyle
Status refers to social honour or prestige, which need not align with economic class
questions.explain: Weber distinguished status, based on social estimation of honour, from class, based on market position, noting the two do not always coincide.

questions.q: Steven Lukes' 'three faces of power' adds which dimension beyond decision-making and non-decision-making?
options: Legal-rational authority
The power to shape people's wants and perceptions so they accept the status quo
Charismatic authority
Economic ownership
questions.explain: Lukes' third face is ideological power: shaping desires and beliefs so people accept arrangements against their real interests.

questions.q: For Marx, the fundamental basis of social class is:
options: Lifestyle and patterns of consumption
Status and prestige in the community
Membership of a particular political party
A person's relationship to the means of production
questions.explain: Marx defined class objectively by ownership (bourgeoisie) or non-ownership (proletariat) of the means of production.

questions.q: Peter Townsend's definition of poverty is best described as:
options: Defined solely by income below the minimum wage
An absolute subsistence standard
Relative deprivation, where people cannot participate in normal activities of their society
Purely a state of welfare dependency
questions.explain: Townsend defined poverty relatively, as resources so far below the average that people are excluded from ordinary living patterns.

questions.q: Goldthorpe and Lockwood's 'Affluent Worker' study (Luton) concluded that affluent manual workers:
options: Had fully merged into the middle class
Had become a revolutionary proletariat
Showed no distinctive class identity
Remained working class but held a privatised, instrumental orientation to work
questions.explain: The study rejected embourgeoisement, finding affluent workers retained a working-class identity but a privatised, money-focused attitude to work.

questions.q: The concept of 'social exclusion' differs from income poverty because it emphasises:
options: Voluntary withdrawal from work
Only a lack of money
Being shut out, fully or partially, from the economic, social and political systems
The same thing as absolute poverty
questions.explain: Social exclusion is a multidimensional process of being marginalised from participation in key institutions of society, not just low income.
